# How to label AI-made videos when you post them on YouTube, TikTok and Facebook

> **In short:** If your video looks real but was made or significantly changed with AI, mark it before you post. On **YouTube**, select **Yes** under **AI use** in the upload details. On **TikTok**, tap **Next**, then **More options**, and turn on **AI-generated content**. On **Facebook**, Meta requires its AI label for photorealistic video or realistic audio that was digitally created or altered.

More and more videos are made or edited with AI: a cloned voice-over, a generated scene, a face swapped into a clip. Viewers deserve to know when something that looks real isn't. YouTube, TikTok and Meta each have their own rules and their own label. This guide describes each one separately, based on that company's own help pages and announcements, so you can follow the rules wherever you post.

## Before you start
-   **The finished video,** and a clear idea of which parts were made or changed with AI.
-   **Your account** on the platform where you'll post.
-   **About 5 minutes per platform.**

## Step 1 — Decide whether your video needs a label
Each company sets its own rules. In general, **realistic** AI content needs a label, and small edits usually don't. Here is what each one says.

**YouTube** says to disclose content that:
-   makes a real person appear to say or do something they didn't,
-   alters footage of a real event or place, or
-   shows a realistic-looking scene that didn't actually happen.

YouTube also asks you to disclose AI music when it's the main focus of the video. It says you don't need to disclose clearly unrealistic or animated content, beauty filters, color or lighting fixes, captions, or using AI only to help write your script, title, or thumbnail.

**TikTok** asks you to label content that was completely generated or significantly edited by AI.

**Meta** (Facebook) requires its label for photorealistic video or realistic-sounding audio that was digitally created or altered.

💬 Example: A clip where your cloned voice reads the narration over real footage → label it. A clip where you only used AI to brainstorm the title → no label needed on YouTube.

You'll know it worked when you can say in one sentence what in your video is AI-made.

## Step 2 — YouTube: turn on "AI use" while uploading
In **YouTube Studio**, start your upload as usual. In the details, find the **Attributes** section. Under **AI use**, select **Yes** if your video needs disclosure.

YouTube says the label then appears in the expanded description, and for some topics in the video player itself. According to YouTube, disclosing on its own won't limit your video's audience or its eligibility to earn money. Creators who repeatedly don't disclose may have a label added by YouTube or face penalties.

You'll know it worked when your video's expanded description shows the label after it's published.

## Step 3 — TikTok: switch on "AI-generated content"
In the **TikTok app**, record or upload your video, then tap **Next**. Tap **More options** and turn on **AI-generated content**. Then post as usual.

On a **computer**, click **Upload**, choose your video, click **See more**, turn on **AI-generated content**, and click **Post**.

TikTok says it may also add a label automatically, for example when you use its own AI effects or when the file carries **Content Credentials** (C2PA) showing it was made with AI. Once a label is on, it can't be removed after posting. Labeled videos still have to follow TikTok's Community Guidelines.

You'll know it worked when your posted video shows TikTok's AI-generated label.

## Step 4 — Facebook: use Meta's AI label before you post
Meta says people must use its AI disclosure and label tool when they post a **photorealistic video** or **realistic-sounding audio** that was digitally created or altered, and that it may apply penalties if they don't. Meta shows these posts with an **AI info** label, and it may add the label itself when it detects industry-standard signals that content was made with AI.

Meta doesn't publish step-by-step screens that we could verify, so here's the safe approach: before you post, look for the AI label option in your post or reel settings and turn it on.

**If it looks different:** If you can't find the option, check Meta's Help Center for the current steps before posting.

You'll know it worked when your published post shows the **AI info** label.

## Common mistakes
-   **Thinking "it's only a little AI" means no label:** A realistic cloned voice or a swapped face counts, even if the rest is real footage.
    *   **The fix:** Use Step 1. If the AI part could make viewers believe something happened that didn't, label it.
-   **Labeling on one platform and forgetting the others:** Each platform has its own switch.
    *   **The fix:** When you post the same video in several places, turn the label on in each one.
-   **Hiding the AI part in the caption only:** A caption alone may not count as the platform's label.
    *   **The fix:** Use the official switch. You can also mention it in the caption.
-   **Using someone else's face or voice without permission:** A label doesn't make that okay.
    *   **The fix:** Only use people's likeness or voice with their clear consent.

## What this means for you
-   **In everyday life:** If you share fun AI clips with friends and family, a label keeps anyone from mistaking them for real events.
-   **For your business or work:** Labeling protects your reputation and helps you follow each platform's rules for realistic AI content.
-   **If you're just getting started:** Make it a habit. Before you post, ask yourself: "Could someone think this really happened?" If yes, switch the label on.

## Try it now
Pick one video you plan to post this week. Write down in one sentence what in it was made with AI, check it against Step 1, and if it needs a label, turn on the switch from Step 2, 3, or 4 when you upload it.
